title: Integrated multi-country results platform
text:
The problem
Each country office reported reach in its own spreadsheet format, on its own schedule. Leadership had no single, current answer to a simple question: how many people are we reaching against our strategy targets? Monthly consolidation took about two weeks of manual copy-and-paste.

title: Integrated multi-country results platform
text:
What I built

 CollectKoboToolbox / ODK forms, SharePoint trackers, Excel workbooks→
 ValidateConstraints at entry, Power Query checks, DQA review→
 ModelStar schema: fact reach, dimension project, country, indicator, date→
 ReportReach vs target dashboards, drill-through by country and project


One data model fed by every source, with shared dimension tables for country, project, indicator and fiscal period (Oct–Sep fiscal year).
Indicator definitions and counting rules documented once and applied in DAX, so every page counts the same way.
Role-based access through Power BI workspaces and SharePoint permissions, so country teams see their data and leadership sees the portfolio.
Companion dashboards on the same pattern: WASH health-facility assessment (ONA/ODK) and an HR staff tracker.

title: Overall Equipment Effectiveness dashboard
text:
ToolPower BI · DAX
 DomainManufacturing efficiency
 PagesOEE · Stoppages
 StatusLive, interactive
Overall Equipment Effectiveness (OEE) is the standard measure of how well a factory uses its machines. It multiplies three ratios: availability (was the machine running?), performance (was it running at full speed?) and quality (were the parts good?). This dashboard shows all three, so a manager can see where the losses come from rather than just how big they are.

title: Overall Equipment Effectiveness dashboard
text:
The dashboard



The OEE page: KPI cards, monthly trend, hours vs runtime, and gauges by machine type.



  

Interactive version above. Use the month and machine-type buttons on the left. If it doesn't load, use Open the live dashboard.

title: Overall Equipment Effectiveness dashboard
text:
What it shows

Takeaway: overall OEE is 61.87%, and availability (72.76%) is the main drag. Performance (85.23%) and quality (99.78%) are strong, so the biggest gain would come from reducing downtime, not from faster or better production.


Availability is the weak link. It starts at 40% in January, holds around 75–77% from February to June (peaking in April), then falls to 67% in July.
Friction machines need attention. They have the lowest OEE (51%), held back by availability of only 60%.
“Other” machines perform best, with OEE of 80% and availability of 95%.
Quality is near-perfect everywhere, at 100% for every machine type.
Hours vs runtime: February and March have the most scheduled hours (2.02K and 1.97K). The gap between total hours and runtime in each month is the downtime that drives availability down.

title: Overall Equipment Effectiveness dashboard
text:
How it’s built

KPI cards with ring charts for OEE and its three components, with change versus the previous period.
Switchable trend chart. Buttons swap the line chart between OEE, availability, performance and quality without leaving the page.
Switchable comparison. The bar chart toggles between total hours vs runtime and planned vs produced quantity.
A gauge matrix, machine type × metric, so the weakest cell stands out in yellow against green.
Button-style slicers for month and machine type, a light/dark theme toggle, and a separate Stoppages page for root-cause detail.

title: From KCSE to Graduation
text:
ToolsR · ggplot2 · ggalluvial · ggridges
 Data6,000 students · 5 universities
 Format4 charts + 5-page storyboard
 Headline70% admitted · 76% graduated
A dark palette drawn from the Kenyan flag, and four chart types, each chosen for one question: a flow diagram for the route, ridgelines for grades, a lollipop histogram for time, and dumbbells for groups.
The charts also work as a data-quality audit. They surface records that can’t be true, and a good analyst says so instead of hiding it.

title: From KCSE to Graduation
text:
01 · The route



Flow from KCSE grade through university admission to graduation.



Takeaway: 1,363 students are recorded as graduating without being admitted, nearly one in three graduates. That points to a data problem, not a policy one.

title: From KCSE to Graduation
text:
02 · The grades



Subject-performance distributions by KCSE mean grade.



Takeaway: an A and a C+ look the same on paper. Every grade spans 50–100%, and the medians sit within about three points of each other.

title: From KCSE to Graduation
text:
03 · The clock



Number of students at each recorded time to graduation.



Takeaway: a third of students sit exactly on the 4-year floor or the 6-year ceiling, a sign the values were capped.

title: From KCSE to Graduation
text:
04 · The groups



Admission and graduation rates by income, region, gender, school type, programme and university.



Takeaway: income, region, gender and school barely move the rates. The widest gaps are “Other” gender (lowest admission) and Harambee schools (highest graduation).

title: From KCSE to Graduation
text:
Design choices

Highlight colour carries meaning. Green marks the expected route and red the anomaly, used the same way in every chart.
Annotate the outliers directly (1,040 students at exactly 4.0 years) instead of leaving readers to find them.
Dark background with the flag stripe for a recognisably Kenyan look.

title: From KCSE to Graduation
text:
The code
All four charts come from one reproducible R script (ggplot2 · ggtext · ggalluvial · ggridges · ragg). It reads data/Kenyan_Students_University_Progression.xlsx and saves each chart as a 300 dpi PNG.
 Download the R script






NoteView the full script (182 lines)





# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Kenyan students: from KCSE grade to university graduation
# Input : data/Kenyan_Students_University_Progression.xlsx (6,000 students)
# Output: k1_flow.png, k2_ridges.png, k3_time.png, k4_groups.png
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(dplyr); library(tidyr); library(readxl); library(forcats); library(ggplot2)
  library(ggtext); library(ggalluvial); library(ggridges); library(scales); library(ragg)
})

f <- list.files("data", pattern = "xlsx$", full.names = TRUE)[1]
d <- read_excel(f)
names(d) <- c("grade", "perf", "ses", "region", "gender", "school", "admit", "program", "grad", "years", "uni")
grades <- c("A", "A-", "B+", "B", "B-", "C+")
d <- d |> mutate(grade = factor(grade, levels = grades))

# ---- Kenyan-flag palette on a dark ground -----------------------------------
bg <- "#101317"; ink <- "#F1EDE4"; mute <- "#8A919C"; faint <- "#262B33"
green <- "#2FA36B"; red <- "#E0413C"; white <- "#E9E4D8"; dim <- "#3A414C"
ttl <- "Inter Display"; txt <- "Inter"

theme_ke <- function(base = 13) {
  theme_minimal(base_size = base, base_family = txt) +
    theme(
      plot.background = element_rect(fill = bg, colour = NA),
      panel.background = element_rect(fill = bg, colour = NA),
      panel.grid = element_blank(),
      plot.title.position = "plot", plot.caption.position = "plot",
      plot.title = element_textbox_simple(family = ttl, face = "bold", size = base * 2.3, colour = ink,
                                          lineheight = 1, margin = margin(b = 8)),
      plot.subtitle = element_textbox_simple(size = base * 1.02, colour = mute, lineheight = 1.3,
                                             margin = margin(b = 22)),
      plot.caption = element_markdown(size = base * .68, colour = mute, hjust = 0, margin = margin(t = 18)),
      axis.text = element_text(colour = mute, size = base * .82),
      axis.title = element_text(colour = mute, size = base * .8),
      legend.position = "none",
      plot.margin = margin(30, 36, 22, 30)
    )
}
cap <- "**Data:** Kenyan Students University Progression · 6,000 students"
save <- function(p, file, w = 13, h = 8) ggsave(file, p, width = w, height = h, dpi = 300, device = agg_png, bg = bg)
hl <- function(x, col) paste0("<b style='color:", col, "'>", x, "</b>")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1 · Flow: KCSE grade -> admitted? -> graduated?
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
fl <- d |>
  mutate(admit = factor(if_else(admit == "yes", "Admitted", "Not admitted"), c("Admitted", "Not admitted")),
         grad  = factor(if_else(grad == "yes", "Graduated", "Did not graduate"), c("Graduated", "Did not graduate")),
         path  = case_when(admit == "Not admitted" & grad == "Graduated" ~ "odd",
                           admit == "Admitted" & grad == "Graduated" ~ "ok",
                           TRUE ~ "out")) |>
  count(grade, admit, grad, path)
n_odd <- sum(fl$n[fl$path == "odd"])

lab_nodes <- tibble(
  x = c(rep(1, 6), 2, 2, 3, 3),
  stratum = c(grades, "Admitted", "Not admitted", "Graduated", "Did not graduate"))

p1 <- ggplot(fl, aes(axis1 = grade, axis2 = admit, axis3 = grad, y = n)) +
  geom_alluvium(aes(fill = path), width = .09, alpha = .78, knot.pos = .42, curve_type = "sigmoid", colour = NA) +
  geom_stratum(width = .09, fill = faint, colour = bg, linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_text(stat = "stratum", aes(label = after_stat(ifelse(x == 1, paste0(stratum, "  ", comma(count)), NA))),
            family = txt, fontface = "bold", colour = ink, size = 3.6, hjust = 1, nudge_x = -.065, na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_label(stat = "stratum", aes(label = after_stat(ifelse(x == 2, paste0(stratum, "\n", comma(count)), NA))),
             family = txt, fontface = "bold", colour = ink, fill = bg, label.size = 0, size = 3.6,
             lineheight = .95, label.padding = unit(.35, "lines"), na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_text(stat = "stratum", aes(label = after_stat(ifelse(x == 3, paste0(stratum, "\n", comma(count)), NA))),
            family = txt, fontface = "bold", colour = ink, size = 3.6, hjust = 0, nudge_x = .065,
            lineheight = .95, na.rm = TRUE) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(ok = green, odd = red, out = dim)) +
  scale_x_discrete(limits = c("KCSE grade", "University admission", "Graduation"), expand = c(.1, .1),
                   position = "top") +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) +
  labs(
    title = paste0("Nearly one in three graduates was ", hl("never admitted", red)),
    subtitle = paste0(
      "6,000 students from KCSE result to graduation. About 70% are admitted at every grade, from A to C+. ",
      hl(paste0(comma(n_odd), " students"), red), " are recorded as not admitted yet still graduated, alongside ",
      hl("3,184 who took the expected route", green), "."),
    x = NULL, y = NULL, caption = cap) +
  theme_ke() +
  coord_cartesian(clip = "off") +
  theme(plot.margin = margin(30, 110, 22, 30), axis.text.y = element_blank(), axis.text.x.top = element_text(colour = ink, face = "bold", size = 12,
                                                                     margin = margin(b = 6)))
save(p1, "k1_flow.png", w = 13, h = 8.2)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2 · Ridgelines: subject performance by KCSE grade
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
meds <- d |> group_by(grade) |> summarise(m = median(perf))
p2 <- ggplot(d, aes(perf, fct_rev(grade))) +
  geom_density_ridges(aes(fill = grade == "A" | grade == "C+"), scale = 1.35, rel_min_height = .003,
                      colour = bg, linewidth = .8, bandwidth = 2.2, alpha = .95) +
  geom_point(data = meds, aes(m, as.numeric(fct_rev(grade)) + .06), shape = 21, size = 3.4,
             fill = bg, colour = ink, stroke = 1.1) +
  geom_text(data = meds, aes(m, as.numeric(fct_rev(grade)) + .36, label = number(m, .1)),
            family = txt, size = 3.2, colour = ink, fontface = "bold") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = green, `FALSE` = dim)) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(45, 105), breaks = seq(50, 100, 10), labels = label_percent(scale = 1)) +
  scale_y_discrete(expand = expansion(add = c(.2, 1.1))) +
  labs(
    title = paste0("An ", hl("A", green), " and a ", hl("C+", green), " look the same on paper"),
    subtitle = "Subject performance by KCSE mean grade. Every grade spans the full range from 50% to 100%, and the medians (rings) sit within about three points of each other.",
    x = "Subject performance", y = NULL, caption = cap) +
  theme_ke() +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_text(colour = ink, face = "bold", size = 15, vjust = 0),
        panel.grid.major.x = element_line(colour = faint, linewidth = .4))
save(p2, "k2_ridges.png", w = 12, h = 8.4)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3 · Time to graduation: every 0.1-year step
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
tt <- d |> mutate(years = round(years, 1)) |> count(years) |> mutate(edge = years %in% c(4, 6))
p3 <- ggplot(tt, aes(years, n)) +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = years, y = 0, yend = n, colour = edge), linewidth = 1.6, lineend = "round") +
  geom_point(aes(colour = edge, size = edge)) +
  annotate("text", x = 4.08, y = 1040, label = "1,040 students at\nexactly 4.0 years", hjust = 0,
           vjust = .9, family = txt, size = 4, colour = red, fontface = "bold", lineheight = .95) +
  annotate("text", x = 5.92, y = 1004, label = "1,004 students at\nexactly 6.0 years", hjust = 1,
           vjust = .9, family = txt, size = 4, colour = red, fontface = "bold", lineheight = .95) +
  annotate("text", x = 5, y = 330, label = "everyone in between: 150–250 per step", family = txt,
           size = 3.6, colour = mute) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = red, `FALSE` = white)) +
  scale_size_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = 5, `FALSE` = 2.6)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(4, 6, .5), labels = \(x) paste0(x, " yrs"), expand = c(.03, .03)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1120), breaks = seq(0, 1000, 250), labels = comma, expand = c(0, 0)) +
  labs(
    title = paste0("Time to graduate piles up at ", hl("the edges", red)),
    subtitle = "Number of students at each recorded time to graduation, in steps of 0.1 years. A third of all students sit exactly on the 4-year floor or the 6-year ceiling, a sign the values were capped.",
    x = NULL, y = "Students", caption = cap) +
  theme_ke() +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_line(colour = faint, linewidth = .4))
save(p3, "k3_time.png", w = 13, h = 7.6)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4 · Every group, admission vs graduation rate
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
vars <- c(ses = "Family income", region = "Region", gender = "Gender", school = "School type",
          program = "Programme", uni = "University")
gr <- lapply(names(vars), \(v) d |> group_by(level = .data[[v]]) |>
               summarise(admit = mean(admit == "yes"), grad = mean(grad == "yes"), n = n()) |>
               mutate(var = vars[[v]])) |>
  bind_rows() |>
  mutate(level = recode(level, high = "High", low = "Low", middle = "Middle", rural = "Rural", urban = "Urban",
                        female = "Female", male = "Male", other = "Other", harambee = "Harambee",
                        private = "Private", public = "Public", humanities = "Humanities",
                        vocational = "Vocational"),
         level = gsub(" University", "", level),
         var = factor(var, levels = vars)) |>
  group_by(var) |> mutate(level = fct_reorder(level, admit)) |> ungroup()

ov <- c(admit = mean(d$admit == "yes"), grad = mean(d$grad == "yes"))
p4 <- ggplot(gr, aes(y = level)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = ov[["admit"]], colour = green, linetype = "dotted", linewidth = .5) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = ov[["grad"]], colour = white, linetype = "dotted", linewidth = .5) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = admit, xend = grad, yend = level), colour = dim, linewidth = 2.4, lineend = "round") +
  geom_point(aes(x = admit), colour = green, size = 4) +
  geom_point(aes(x = grad), colour = white, size = 4) +
  geom_text(data = filter(gr, level %in% c("Other", "Harambee")),
            aes(x = if_else(level == "Other", admit - .006, grad + .006), label = percent(if_else(level == "Other", admit, grad), .1),
                hjust = if_else(level == "Other", 1, 0)),
            family = txt, size = 3.4, fontface = "bold", colour = ink) +
  facet_grid(var ~ ., scales = "free_y", space = "free_y", switch = "y") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(.6, .84), breaks = seq(.6, .8, .05), labels = label_percent(),
                     position = "top") +
  labs(
    title = "Income, region, gender or school: the rates barely move",
    subtitle = paste0(hl("Admission rate", green), " and ", hl("graduation rate", white),
                      " for every group in the data. Nearly all sit within a few points of the overall rates (dotted lines). ",
                      "The widest gaps: students recorded as ", hl("Other", ink), " gender are admitted least, and ",
                      hl("Harambee", ink), " school students graduate most."),
    x = NULL, y = NULL, caption = cap) +
  theme_ke() +
  theme(strip.placement = "outside",
        strip.text.y.left = element_text(angle = 0, hjust = 1, colour = mute, size = 10, face = "bold",
                                         margin = margin(r = 14)),
        panel.spacing.y = unit(.9, "lines"),
        panel.grid.major.x = element_line(colour = faint, linewidth = .4),
        axis.text.y = element_text(colour = ink, size = 10.5))
save(p4, "k4_groups.png", w = 12, h = 10)
message("Done")

title: Beneficiary deduplication model in DAX
text:
The problem
One person can receive several services from several projects in one year. Summing reach across projects overstates the portfolio, which is a credibility risk in donor reporting.

title: Beneficiary deduplication model in DAX
text:
Approach

Define the unit of count for each indicator: unique individual, household or service contact.
Build a stable person key from available identifiers, with fallbacks when IDs are missing.
Apply counting rules in the model, not in the visuals, so every report inherits them.
Show both views: total services delivered and unique people reached, with the gap made visible.

Unique Beneficiaries Reached =
CALCULATE (
    DISTINCTCOUNT ( Reach[PersonKey] ),
    Reach[CountingRule] = "Unique individual",
    REMOVEFILTERS ( Reach[Service] )
)

Double-count Avoided =
[Total Service Contacts] - [Unique Beneficiaries Reached]

title: Beneficiary deduplication model in DAX
text:
Impact

Reach figures follow written counting rules that donors can check.
Projects and services can be combined without inflating totals.

Custom Power BI visuals with Deneb
text:
ToolsPower BI · Deneb · Vega-Lite
 VisualsHeatmap · small multiples
 Why DenebCharts Power BI can't do natively
 Format2-page storyboard
Power BI’s built-in visuals cover the basics. Deneb lets me write Vega-Lite specs inside a report, so I can build custom layouts that still filter, cross-highlight and refresh like any other visual.

title: Custom Power BI visuals with Deneb
section: Visual 1 · Arizona’s drought, week by week
text:
Visual 1 · Arizona’s drought, week by week



Fifteen Arizona counties, one row each, January 2020 to mid-2022. Each cell is one week, coloured by the Drought Severity and Coverage Index.



What stands out: drought arrives together. Almost every county darkens in the same weeks around August–October 2020, stays severe until July 2021, then eases sharply with the summer rains. Mohave holds on longest.

How it’s built: rect marks on a week × county grid, with a quantized colour scale in five steps so each shade means one severity level. A thin gap between cells keeps individual weeks readable without gridlines.

title: Custom Power BI visuals with Deneb
text:
Visual 2 · Energy under changing skies



53 weekly tiles of energy use. Dark area is power from the grid, orange is solar used, and the dot is solar generated. Hovering opens a detail panel.



What stands out: two halves of the year. Weeks 1–21 are low and flat, and from week 22 demand jumps into tall peaks. Solar covers only a thin layer, and the sunniest weeks fall in the quietest period.

How it’s built: faceted area charts (one facet per week) with layered grid and solar areas and a sized circle for weekly generation. The hover panel combines a flow diagram and daily stacked bars.

title: Same Money, Same Scores?
text:
ToolsR · ggplot2 · ggtext
 Data1,000 schools · 10 US states
 Format4 charts + 5-page storyboard
 FindingNo real gap by type, funding or poverty
The usual story about schools is that money and income decide results. This dataset says otherwise. Across every cut I tried, scores sit close to 70%. The design challenge was to show a flat result honestly, letting the absence of a gap be the headline rather than inventing one.

title: Same Money, Same Scores?
text:
Frame 1 · Start with the scores



Every school is a dot. The bar spans the middle half of schools, and the ring marks the median.



Takeaway: medians are 71.4% (public), 70.5% (private) and 67.0% (charter), but the spread within each type dwarfs the gap between them (Kruskal–Wallis p = 0.52).

title: Same Money, Same Scores?
text:
Frame 2 · Follow the money



Funding per student against test scores, one panel per school type, with a trend line.



Takeaway: spending five times more per student barely moves scores. Only private schools tilt upward, about 3 points per extra $10,000, and funding explains around 1% of the variation.

title: Same Money, Same Scores?
section: Frame 3 · Does poverty change the picture?
text:
Frame 3 · Does poverty change the picture?



Schools split into quarters by share of low-income students and by funding. Each tile shows the average score.



Takeaway: all 16 groups average between 67% and 73%. The poorest, least-funded group (70.6%) scores about the same as the best-off, best-funded group (70.0%). That’s unusual next to most real-world studies.

title: Same Money, Same Scores?
text:
Frame 4 · Where a school is



State averages for funding and test scores, with 95% confidence intervals.



Takeaway: California (73.9%) and Ohio (65.8%) are the only clear gap. Spending and results don’t line up: Texas is the second-lowest spender but ranks 4th on scores.

title: Same Money, Same Scores?
text:
Design choices

Titles state the finding, so a reader who sees only the headline still gets the point.
Colour replaces the legend. School types are coloured inside the subtitle text with ggtext.
Uncertainty is visible. Interquartile bars, trend-line bands and confidence intervals show how sure each comparison is.
One warm, quiet palette across all four frames, so the set reads as a single story.

title: Same Money, Same Scores?
text:
The code
All four charts come from one reproducible R script (ggplot2 · ggtext · ggbeeswarm · patchwork · ragg). It reads data/education_inequality_data.csv and saves each chart as a 300 dpi PNG.
 Download the R script






NoteView the full script (194 lines)





# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# School funding, performance and access across public, private and charter
# schools: four charts in ggplot2.
# Input : data/education_inequality_data.csv (1,000 schools, 10 states)
# Output: 01_scores_by_type.png ... 04_states.png
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(dplyr); library(tidyr); library(readr); library(forcats)
  library(ggplot2); library(ggtext); library(ggbeeswarm); library(patchwork)
  library(scales); library(ragg)
})

d <- read_csv("data/education_inequality_data.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(school_type = factor(school_type, levels = c("Public", "Private", "Charter")))

# ---- Look & feel ----------------------------------------------------------
pal <- c(Public = "#2F5D8C", Private = "#D1603D", Charter = "#3B8C6E")
bg  <- "#FBF8F3"; ink <- "#1F2430"; mute <- "#7A7F8C"; grid <- "#E8E2D8"
font <- "Inter"

col_txt <- function(x, col = pal[x]) glue::glue("<b style='color:{col}'>{x}</b>")

theme_edu <- function(base = 13) {
  theme_minimal(base_size = base, base_family = font) +
    theme(
      plot.background  = element_rect(fill = bg, colour = NA),
      panel.background = element_rect(fill = bg, colour = NA),
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      panel.grid.major = element_line(colour = grid, linewidth = .35),
      plot.title.position = "plot", plot.caption.position = "plot",
      plot.title    = element_textbox_simple(size = base * 1.75, face = "bold", colour = ink,
                                             lineheight = 1.05, margin = margin(b = 14)),
      plot.subtitle = element_textbox_simple(size = base * .98, colour = mute, lineheight = 1.3,
                                             margin = margin(b = 18)),
      plot.caption  = element_textbox_simple(size = base * .7, colour = mute, lineheight = 1.25,
                                             margin = margin(t = 16)),
      axis.title  = element_text(colour = mute, size = base * .8),
      axis.text   = element_text(colour = mute, size = base * .8),
      strip.text  = element_markdown(size = base * 1.05, hjust = 0, margin = margin(b = 6)),
      legend.position = "none",
      plot.margin = margin(28, 32, 20, 28)
    )
}
src <- "**Data:** education_inequality_data.csv · 1,000 schools in 10 US states"
save <- function(p, file, w = 11, h = 7.5) ggsave(file, p, width = w, height = h, dpi = 300, device = agg_png, bg = bg)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1 · Test scores by school type: every school, plus the median
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
kw  <- kruskal.test(avg_test_score_percent ~ school_type, d)
med <- d |> group_by(school_type) |>
  summarise(m = median(avg_test_score_percent), q1 = quantile(avg_test_score_percent, .25),
            q3 = quantile(avg_test_score_percent, .75), n = n())

p1 <- ggplot(d, aes(avg_test_score_percent, fct_rev(school_type), colour = school_type)) +
  geom_quasirandom(orientation = "y", width = .32, size = 1.6, alpha = .45, stroke = 0) +
  geom_linerange(data = med, aes(x = NULL, xmin = q1, xmax = q3, y = fct_rev(school_type)),
                 linewidth = 3.2, colour = ink, alpha = .85, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  geom_point(data = med, aes(x = m), size = 5.2, shape = 21, fill = bg, colour = ink, stroke = 1.4) +
  geom_text(data = med, aes(x = m, label = paste0("median ", number(m, .1), "%")),
            nudge_y = .46, family = font, fontface = "bold", size = 4, colour = ink) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = pal) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(38, 102), breaks = seq(40, 100, 10), labels = label_percent(scale = 1),
                     expand = c(0, 0)) +
  scale_y_discrete(labels = \(x) col_txt(x)) +
  labs(
    title = "Whatever the school type, the typical test score is about 70%",
    subtitle = glue::glue(
      "Each dot is one school. The black bar spans the middle half of schools and the ring marks the median. ",
      "{col_txt('Public')} and {col_txt('Private')} medians sit within one point of each other, and ",
      "{col_txt('Charter')} schools only 4 points lower — a gap smaller than the spread inside any one group ",
      "(Kruskal–Wallis p = {number(kw$p.value, .01)})."),
    x = "Average test score", y = NULL, caption = src) +
  theme_edu() +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_markdown(size = 15), panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())
save(p1, "01_scores_by_type.png", h = 7)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2 · Funding per student vs test score, one panel per school type
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
rs <- d |> group_by(school_type) |>
  summarise(r = cor(funding_per_student_usd, avg_test_score_percent),
            slope = coef(lm(avg_test_score_percent ~ I(funding_per_student_usd / 10000)))[2])

strip_lab <- setNames(
  glue::glue("{col_txt(as.character(rs$school_type))}<span style='color:{mute}'>  ·  r = {sub('^[+-]0.00$', '0.00', sprintf('%+.2f', rs$r))}</span>"),
  rs$school_type)

p2 <- ggplot(d, aes(funding_per_student_usd, avg_test_score_percent, colour = school_type)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = mean(d$avg_test_score_percent), colour = mute, linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_point(size = 1.7, alpha = .4, stroke = 0) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = TRUE, linewidth = 1.3, fill = "grey70", alpha = .35) +
  geom_text(data = rs, aes(x = 24800, y = 104,
                           label = paste0(sprintf("%+.1f", slope), " pts per extra $10k")),
            hjust = 1, family = font, size = 3.6, colour = ink, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~school_type, labeller = as_labeller(strip_lab)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = pal) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_dollar(scale = 1e-3, suffix = "k"), breaks = seq(5000, 25000, 5000)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_percent(scale = 1), limits = c(38, 106), breaks = seq(40, 100, 20)) +
  labs(
    title = "Spending five times more per student barely moves test scores",
    subtitle = glue::glue(
      "Funding runs from about $5,000 to $25,000 per student. For {col_txt('Public')} and {col_txt('Charter')} schools ",
      "the trend is flat. {col_txt('Private')} schools tilt slightly upward (about 3 points per extra $10,000, p = 0.04), ",
      "but funding still explains only about 1% of the variation in their scores. The dotted line is the overall average (70%)."),
    x = "Funding per student", y = "Average test score", caption = src) +
  theme_edu() +
  theme(panel.spacing.x = unit(2.2, "lines"))
save(p2, "02_funding_vs_scores.png", w = 12, h = 6.8)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3 · Poverty x funding grid: average score in each cell
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
qlab_f <- c("Lowest\nfunding", "", "", "Highest\nfunding")
grid3 <- d |>
  mutate(fq = ntile(funding_per_student_usd, 4), lq = ntile(percent_low_income, 4)) |>
  group_by(fq, lq) |>
  summarise(score = mean(avg_test_score_percent), n = n(), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(dev = score - mean(d$avg_test_score_percent))

fr <- d |> mutate(fq = ntile(funding_per_student_usd, 4)) |> group_by(fq) |>
  summarise(lo = min(funding_per_student_usd), hi = max(funding_per_student_usd)) |>
  mutate(lab = paste0(dollar(lo, scale = 1e-3, suffix = "k", accuracy = 1), "–",
                      dollar(hi, scale = 1e-3, suffix = "k", accuracy = 1)))
lr <- d |> mutate(lq = ntile(percent_low_income, 4)) |> group_by(lq) |>
  summarise(lo = min(percent_low_income), hi = max(percent_low_income)) |>
  mutate(lab = paste0(round(lo), "–", round(hi), "%"))

p3 <- ggplot(grid3, aes(lq, fq, fill = dev)) +
  geom_tile(colour = bg, linewidth = 3, width = .96, height = .92) +
  geom_text(aes(label = number(score, .1)), family = font, fontface = "bold", size = 7.5, colour = ink,
            nudge_y = .08) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(n, " schools")), family = font, size = 3.3, colour = mute, nudge_y = -.22) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#C0573A", mid = "#F4EEE4", high = "#2F7A8C", midpoint = 0,
                       limits = c(-15, 15), guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:4, labels = paste0(c("Least poor\n", "", "", "Most poor\n"), lr$lab),
                     expand = c(0, 0), position = "top") +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = 1:4, labels = paste0(qlab_f, ifelse(qlab_f == "", "", "\n"), fr$lab),
                     expand = c(0, 0)) +
  coord_fixed(ratio = .62) +
  labs(
    title = "Rich or poor, well funded or not, scores barely move",
    subtitle = paste0(
      "Schools split into quarters by share of low-income students (across) and funding per student (up). ",
      "Each tile is the average test score. Every cell lands between 67% and 73%. The colour scale runs ",
      "±15 points around the overall average, so the pale tiles show how small the differences are."),
    x = "Share of students from low-income families", y = "Funding per student", caption = src) +
  theme_edu() +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(), axis.ticks = element_blank(), axis.text = element_text(size = 11, colour = ink, lineheight = 1.1),
        axis.title.x.top = element_text(margin = margin(b = 8)))
save(p3, "03_poverty_funding_grid.png", w = 10, h = 8.4)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4 · States: average funding and average score with 95% intervals
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
ci <- function(x) { m <- mean(x); se <- sd(x) / sqrt(length(x)); tibble(m = m, lo = m - 1.96 * se, hi = m + 1.96 * se) }
st <- d |> group_by(state) |>
  reframe(var = c("fund", "score"),
          bind_rows(ci(funding_per_student_usd), ci(avg_test_score_percent)), n = n()) |>
  group_by(var) |> mutate(top = m == max(m), bot = m == min(m)) |> ungroup()
ord <- st |> filter(var == "score") |> arrange(m) |> pull(state)
st <- st |> mutate(state = factor(state, levels = ord))
nat <- c(fund = mean(d$funding_per_student_usd), score = mean(d$avg_test_score_percent))

panel <- function(v, xlab, fmt, hl) {
  dd <- st |> filter(var == v)
  ggplot(dd, aes(m, state)) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = nat[[v]], colour = mute, linetype = "dotted") +
    geom_linerange(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi), linewidth = 2.6, colour = "#D9D1C4", lineend = "round") +
    geom_point(aes(fill = top | bot), shape = 21, size = 4.2, colour = ink, stroke = .8) +
    geom_text(data = filter(dd, top | bot), aes(label = fmt(m)), nudge_y = .42,
              family = font, size = 3.6, fontface = "bold", colour = ink) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = hl, `FALSE` = bg)) +
    scale_x_continuous(labels = fmt) +
    labs(x = xlab, y = NULL) +
    theme_edu() + theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(), axis.text.y = element_text(colour = ink, size = 12))
}
p4a <- panel("fund", "Average funding per student", label_dollar(scale = 1e-3, suffix = "k", accuracy = .1), "#C9A227")
p4b <- panel("score", "Average test score", label_percent(scale = 1, accuracy = .1), "#2F7A8C") +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank())

p4 <- (p4a | p4b) + plot_annotation(
  title = "California tops the test-score table and Ohio sits last, but the gaps are small and uncertain",
  subtitle = paste0(
    "State averages with 95% confidence intervals (grey bars), ordered by test score. Dotted lines mark the ",
    "average across all 1,000 schools. California leads Ohio by 8 points, but most states' intervals overlap. ",
    "Funding ranks don't line up with score ranks: Texas is the second-lowest spender yet ranks 4th on scores, while ",
    "Georgia spends almost as much as top spender New York and ranks 5th."),
  caption = paste0(src, " · Intervals: mean ± 1.96 standard errors"),
  theme = theme_edu())
save(p4, "04_states.png", w = 12, h = 7.6)

message("Done")

title: ONA → KoboToolbox migration pipeline
text:
The problem
Programmes were moving from ONA to KoboToolbox. Re-entering historical submissions by hand was not an option, and neither was losing them.

title: ONA → KoboToolbox migration pipeline
text:
Pipeline

 1 · ExportPull submissions and media from ONA with ODK Briefcase→
 2 · MatchDeploy the same XLSForm on Kobo and check field names line up→
 3 · UploadPython notebook posts each submission XML to the Kobo API→
 4 · ReconcileCompare counts and IDs, source against target

import requests, pathlib

KOBO = "https://kf.kobotoolbox.org"
headers = {"Authorization": f"Token {API_TOKEN}"}

for xml in pathlib.Path("briefcase/instances").rglob("submission.xml"):
    files = {"xml_submission_file": open(xml, "rb")}
    # attach media saved next to the submission
    for m in xml.parent.glob("*.jpg"):
        files[m.name] = open(m, "rb")
    r = requests.post(f"{KOBO}/api/v1/submissions", headers=headers, files=files)
    log(xml.parent.name, r.status_code)
Simplified for illustration. The production notebook adds retries, duplicate checks and a reconciliation report.
